title: A Common Diabetes Drug Just Prevented Heart Failure in People Carrying a Genetic Time Bomb.
excerpt: Harvard and MIT researchers found that dapagliflozin cut heart failure hospitalisations by 82 per cent in carriers of cardiomyopathy gene variants. Most had no idea they were at risk.
body:
For years, identifying a genetic variant for cardiomyopathy meant telling a patient they were at high risk and then having nothing specific to offer them. A study published in Nature Medicine has changed that calculation.

Researchers from Harvard Medical School, Mass General Brigham and MIT analysed whole-exome sequencing data from 12,685 adults with type 2 diabetes enrolled in the DECLARE-TIMI 58 trial, one of the landmark clinical trials for dapagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor commonly prescribed for diabetes. Among them, 121 carried pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in genes associated with cardiomyopathy — dilated, hypertrophic or arrhythmogenic forms of the progressive heart muscle disease.

Over a median follow-up of 4.2 years, dapagliflozin reduced hospitalisations for heart failure by 82 per cent in genetic variant carriers, compared to those receiving a placebo. The absolute risk reduction was 13 percentage points in carriers versus just one percentage point in non-carriers.

The numbers were even more striking in one subgroup. Among the 82 per cent of carriers who had no prior history of heart failure, 12.8 per cent in the placebo group went on to develop it. Among those receiving dapagliflozin: zero.

"Historically, identifying a genetic variant for cardiomyopathy mostly meant telling a patient they were at high risk and not having a specific preventive therapy to offer," said co-lead author Shinwan Kany, a visiting scientist at the Cardiovascular Research Center at Mass General Brigham. "These data show we do have tools to lower risk in these individuals."

## What SGLT2 Inhibitors Actually Do

Dapagliflozin belongs to a class of drugs called SGLT2 inhibitors, originally designed to help diabetic patients excrete excess glucose through the kidneys. Over the past decade, large clinical trials have repeatedly shown that these drugs also protect the heart and kidneys in ways that go beyond blood sugar control — reducing fluid overload, improving cardiac energy metabolism and lowering inflammation.

What this study adds is the genetic dimension. Cardiomyopathy variants are not rare curiosities — they appear in roughly one per cent of the general population and are a leading cause of heart failure in people under 50. Many carriers live for decades without symptoms, unaware that their heart muscle is slowly weakening until it fails.

"Cardiomyopathy variants represent an actionable genotype which can be used to identify patients who derive a larger benefit from dapagliflozin," said co-lead author Nicholas Marston, a cardiologist at Mass General Brigham. "This is especially relevant for patients without established heart failure, where such treatment may not be otherwise initiated."

## Why South Asians Should Pay Attention

The intersection of genetics and diabetes makes this finding acutely relevant for the Indian diaspora. South Asians develop type 2 diabetes at younger ages, at lower body weights and at higher rates than almost any other ethnic group. A 2023 meta-analysis in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology estimated that the age-standardised prevalence of diabetes among South Asians exceeds 15 per cent — more than double the global average.

That means a disproportionately large number of South Asians are already taking or being considered for SGLT2 inhibitors. The question this study raises is whether genetic screening should be added to the decision tree. If you carry a cardiomyopathy variant and already have type 2 diabetes, the evidence now says dapagliflozin could prevent your heart from failing before you ever knew it was in danger.

The caveat is important: all participants in this trial had type 2 diabetes, so the findings cannot yet be extended to carriers without diabetes. The researchers call explicitly for a prospective trial in that population.

## The Bigger Picture: Pharmacogenomics Arrives

This study is part of a broader shift in medicine from treating diseases after they appear to intercepting them at the genetic level. Pharmacogenomics — the science of matching drugs to genotypes — has been a promise for two decades. Studies like this one are beginning to deliver on it.

For NRI families, the practical implication is worth discussing with a cardiologist: if you have type 2 diabetes and a family history of unexplained heart failure, cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death, genetic testing for cardiomyopathy variants may now be medically actionable, not just informational.

The drug already exists. The genetics already exist. What was missing was the evidence connecting the two. That gap just closed.
